# PRDs and requirements

Establish who will use the document and for what decision: product alignment, implementation, design, QA or approval. Lead with the relevant problem, decision or requirement; do not impose a sales introduction.

Separate confirmed requirements, proposals, assumptions and open decisions. Preserve the supplied normative strength (must, should, may), numbers, units, eligibility, roles, states and timing. Use one consistent term per concept; repeated terminology is often necessary. Do not soften requirements into aspirations or invent implementation behavior to make the document look complete.

Where the brief supports it, make behavior testable: actor, starting conditions, action, expected result and relevant exceptions. Address acceptance criteria, permissions, failure states, dependencies and scope only to the extent requested and supported. Label unresolved cases explicitly; propose options as proposals, never as agreed requirements.

If a missing decision blocks meaningful implementation, ask for it or provide a bounded draft with the blocker visible. Do not ask about every conceivable edge case before making progress. For a narrow copy edit, preserve structure and flag material ambiguity without redesigning the specification.

Review whether an engineer and tester could reach the same interpretation. Concision must not remove exceptions, conditions, acceptance criteria or uncertainty. Use document-production skills only when the requested artifact requires them.
